text.p: Following are the main stories in Croatian newspapers on Friday.
- Croatian Defence Minister Gojko Susak and his Slovak counterpart Jan Sitek signed agreement on military cooperation in Bratislava.
- The government proclaims March 24 a day of mourning in the memory of victims of 1991-95 war in Croatia.

- Editorial: Foreign Minister Mate Granic's visit to London showed relations between Croatia and Great Britain have warmed up. The British have changed their attitude towards Croatian independence and no longer seek regional approach to Balkans.

- By redrawing municipal boundaries in Eastern Slavonia for local elections, U.N. Transitional Administrator for the enclave Jacques Klein violated Croatian constitution, claims the opposition Social Liberal party.
- Head of the Croatian Party of Rights slate in Karlovac County, Zdravko Ninkovic, was shot dead in a brawl. Police claimed there are no indications this was a political murder.

- January exports totalled $483.9 million, up 24.2 percent from the same month last year while exports to European Union countries were $255.6 million, up 10.2 percent. Imports at $652.5 million were 23.8 percent higher than in January 1996.
- Croatia has won a new three-year loan programme in support of its economic reforms from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa said.
- New U.S. ambassador to Croatia who will replace Peter Galbraith will be career diplomat who now based in Brussels.
- Some banks, like Karlovacka and Rijecka, might follow in the footsteps of Varazdinska Banka and deblock pre-1991 foreign exchange deposits to attract depositors.
- International Tourist Bourse recently held in Berlin showed Croatia can expect at least 600,000 German tourists this summer.
- Foreign Ministry decided to evacuate some diplomatic staff from Albania and advised citizens against travelling there.

- Croatian journalists' association held a commemoration for Sinisa Glavasevic, famous radio journalist who went missing during 1991 Serb siege of Vukovar. He was identified as one of the victims whose remains were found in the Ovcara mass grave.

- Bosnian Croats have no documents demanded by U.N. war crimes tribunal. Their armed forces, Croatian Defence Council (HVO), were not organised as typical army so no archives existed, says Kresimir Zubak, president of Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation.
- Zagreb county court has started investigation against Mladen Naletilic, also known as Tuta, and Vinko Martinovic, also known as Stela, both Croat warlords in Mostar.
